In the chilling silence of a serene campground, Ernest meets his untimely end by a crowbar; now, it's up to the keen instincts of Detective Winston to unravel the mystery with only two suspects: Addison and Octavia.

Winston found himself by the cars. Addison, the mechanic apprentice, was working under the car hood. He flipped through a book that was on a nearby table while working. Every time he paused to point out something in the room, like the faded motivational posters on the wall or the cozy layout of the waiting area, Winston chuckled. Addison always had an eye for room decor.

"Hard at work I see." Winston said, breaking the silence. 

Addison shut the book and turned to face him. "The work never ends," he replied, looking Winston up and down. 

"I hear you were at the same camping site as Ernest. He was found murdered there." Winston shared. 

"Work, school, camping... always busy." Addison replied, his gaze wandering again. He'd developed a habit - one even his fellow students noticed during lunch breaks and in every class - of constantly looking around at different parts of the room. 

Winston noticed that tendency walked hand in hand with his need to stay busy, like a curious mind reaching for unknown boundaries. 'Just like him to always have his nose in a book even during lunch breaks', he thought.

"But it's not always just work and school, right?" Winston asked. "You also attend those parties out in the campground, yeah?" There had been a big one on the night of the murder.

Addison picked the book off the table and flipped through the pages, shrugging nonchalantly. "Yeah, I was there. So was half the town. Doesn't mean I know anything about what happened to Ernest. That party was big, a lot could've happened."

Next to Addison, Winston noticed an array of tools lined up on the workbench. Screwdrivers, hammers, and a crowbar among others, which was casually left on the side of the workbench. He'd seen Addison regularly with his work tools, it was part of being an apprentice.

"So, you're a mechanic apprentice, right?" Winston asked. "You work with these kinds of tools every day?"

Addison looked at him for a moment before nodding. "That's right. It's my field of work. Handling tools like crowbars is just part of the job."

Winston left Addison with his book and his workshop, making his way out to his car.

Camping, tool handling, busy campgrounds... Winston had a lot to think about on the drive back to the station. But, as always, the detective knew better than to rush to any conclusions just yet. The only thing certain was that everyone he met added a new piece to the puzzle. That was the nature of his job, chasing the truth and sifting through the fragments of life his line of work offered him. Little by little, every witness, every suspect, and every victim told their own part of the story.

Winston watched Octavia’s firm grip around her mug of lukewarm coffee. She was a sturdy woman, her experience in construction before joining the police force wasn't common knowledge, but it gave her that burly silhouette. He also knew that she had picked up a knack for handling construction tools, crowbars included, from her watch in the building business.

"Officer Octavia," started Winston, trying to appear casual, "Officer 'tavia," he corrected himself, as per the way locals referred to her, "you were on patrol the night Ernest was murdered, correct?"

Her gaze remained steady, not threatening nor hesitant, "Yes, that would be right."

"Were the campgrounds along your route?" asked Winston, knowing that he was treading on thin ice. The campgrounds which were part of her regular beat were also where poor Ernest was found dead.

"They sure were," she replied without diverting her gaze. "I've patrolled there for years now."

Winston pressed on, “Ernest, a known revealer of secrets, was threatening to leak his current findings. He'd uncovered an officer’s shady past and he claimed it was yours. Know anything about that?”

Octavia just looked through him, her facial muscles taut as she remained stoic. "Ernest was always digging around for information, but I can't say I do."

Staying strategic, he continued, "Ernest indicated that this officer with supposed shady practices was involved in illegal activities before joining the force. Oddly reminiscent of your own construction and police career, Octavia. Fearful of any skeletons in the closet that might be found?”

Here, Octavia's mask seemed to crack, but just for a moment, "I've no idea what you're implying."

Winston chose his next words carefully, conscious of her legal knowledge, “Do you have access to a crowbar, officer Octavia?”

She let out a short laugh, a sarcastic retort forming on her lips, “Well, every police department has its set of tools, Winston. Are you implying because we have crowbars, we might be swinging them at the locals?”

Winston remained silent, letting Octavia’s scoff hang in the air before speaking again. He gently changed the direction of his questions, “During your patrol last night, did you happen to see anything out of ordinary at the camp?”

“Just a quiet starry night, nothing too wild happening in my town, Winston.”

As the conversation winded up, Winston decided to leave Octavia with one last piece of thought, “Ernest had hinted at uncovering a cop's illegal past, may be yours. It does seem like there’s something you’d want to keep from the force.”

For the first time during their conversation, Octavia looked unsure. She shook her head, "I couldn't tell you, Winston."

As an investigative officer himself, Winston knew the camaraderie among the police ranks. Tonight he’d heard enough. He’d got Octavia talking, about her quiet patrol night and the secret that she urgently seemed to want buried, and her past involvement in illegal activities. As he left Octavia’s living room, he could not help but wonder more about this lady cop with a knack for using crowbars.

In the serene isolation of a snow-draped chalet, Harry's life is abruptly ended by the vicious snap of a bear trap; now, it's up to the astute Detective Winston to unravel the deadly web spun by the questionable duo, Dexter and Gordon.

Winston, drizzly and cold from the rain, squinted at the farmhouse across the gloomy countryside. The hunting shop sign creaking in the wind was a well-known fixture having Gordon's name inscribed in bold on the top. Winston knew very well that the shop was run by Gordon, who was as good a supplier of hunting equipment as he was a farmer. The murder of Harry, now known in newspapers as "The Chalet Bear Trap Murder," had to be untangled.

In front of Winston, a rough-faced man, smeared with sweat and dust from his work at both the shop and the farm, set to work, carrying feed bags to the barn. It was Gordon, the local farmer in question.

"Hello, Gordon," - Winston greeted him.

"Howdy, got no time to chat. Gotta feed the animals before the weather worsens. These parts, we got some bear problems," - Gordon grunted in response.

Catching a break, Winston moved towards the subject. "I heard you had some form of disagreement with Harry at the farmer's market a while back."

Scoffing, Gordon refused to meet his gaze. "Sure, we had words... I wasn't selling much, and he was selling everything. Fella won an award recently for his agricultural products while the market for my products was going under."

"You blame Harry for that?" - Winston asked, laying the facts bare.

"Goddam right I do..." - Gordon muttered, throwing a dirty sack onto a pile.

"Where were you at the time Harry was killed, Gordon?"

The farmer dusted his hands, meeting Winston's gaze with defiance. "I was here, at the farm. All day. You can ask anyone around."

“As for the chalet where poor Harry met his end..." - Winston started.

“Yeah, Harry was at my chalet. It’s my property, and I’m the who decides who can or can't access it." - Gordon interrupted, more flustered now.

"Did you see anyone else around that day?"

"Nope. Quiet as a mouse that day, just the bears and me."

After that, silence fell over the now dark homestead. Winston considered the facts, the countryside, farm, bears, the market, the struggling sales, it all called for further investigation. But for now, he just tipped his hat and walked back to his car under the drizzling rain, leaving a brooding Gordon to his work.

As the sheer size of the chalet murder scene could overwhelm a lesser detective, Winston, stood firm. The victim, Harry, was a known critic within the food industry. His sharp tongue had a penchant for landing him in a hot stew of trouble. This time, it would seem, there was a rogue ingredient he just couldn't swallow.

Winston strolled over to Dexter, a known acquaintance of Harry's and an avid food enthusiast himself. The man's love for fine cuisine was matched only by his fervour for his religion.

"Evening, Dexter," Winston began. "How are you holding up?"

"I'm doing okay... under the circumstances." Dexter wasn't the most expressive despite his harsh critiques.

"I heard Harry was very open about his thoughts on your religious beliefs," Winston continued.

Dexter sighed, "Yes, he publicly mocked my faith during an event. Disrespectful, but that was just Harry."

"Dexter," Winston turned back to him, "I noticed a photograph of you and Tony the Tooth having dinner together surfaced on social media. Where were you the night of Harry's death?"

"I... I was there, having dinner with Tony, known to his friends as 'Tony the Tooth,' I've recently learned."

Winston paused at the mention of that name. Tony the Tooth’s reputation proceeded him. Known as a racketeer and money launderer, his guilty verdict in a recent court case was infamous. Dexter's association with him, especially in a photograph in a restaurant notoriously frequented by other criminals, only bred more suspicion.

Changing tactics, Winston delved into Dexter's rural interests. Dexter's love for hunting was no secret to the community; he was often seen in the woods around the outskirts of the town. Dexter was not only known for his hobby of collecting hunting equipment but also for his knowledge of various hunting techniques. One of the common pieces of equipment in his collection was bear traps, which he frequently used in the woods. Dexter was often seen studying these traps, enhancing his understanding of them.

"Care to show me your hunting gear?" Winston suddenly asked, catching him off guard.

"Sure, I guess," Dexter replied tensely. He led the way to a shed, where hunting equipment including rifles and the commonly used bear traps littered the floor and walls.

"It's quite the collection," Dexter added, trying to read Winston's face.

Winston, however, didn't respond. He scribbled down a few more notes before thanking Dexter for his time and heading back to his car. His head was awash with the evening's revelations, notably Dexter's disrespect and his surprising dinner partner.

Target case file:

In the grim underbelly of the wrestling world, Eleanor meets her shocking end by a halberd, leaving Detective Winston to untangle a web of deception spun by Elizabeth and Freya.

Eleanor was to be the star of the show. After all, she was is in high demand, even other directors wanted her, luring her with offers. Yet with loss and betrayal, her world was cut short in a wrestling ring of all places. By a halberd, an ancient weapon, now primarily a theatrical prop.

Taking a deep breath, Detective Winston perused his notes. It highlighted a complex web of deceit and jealousy, one that placed Elizabeth, the director of the play, at its center. As director, she possessed keys to every corner of the premises, from mundane storage rooms to the wrestling stage utilized for rehearsals. He noted that the wrestling ring was near the storage, where the halberd used in rehearsals was kept. Throughout the rehearsal process, Elizabeth personally supervised the handling and usage of the props. The halberd, in particular, was a focal point of the performance.

His mind swarmed back to the crime scene, the wrestling ring...currently cordoned off with police tape. Eleanor's lifeless body sprawled under the unforgiving ring lights.

Earlier, Elizabeth was overseeing the wrestling rehearsals. At one point, she had asked everyone else to leave the wrestling ring area. Not long after, Eleanor was found dead. It was a shocking scene, a terrible ending to a tense day.

Recalling his earlier conversation with Elizabeth, he remembered her mentioning a confrontation with Eleanor. She was upset, angry that Eleanor was having an affair with her husband. Yet Eleanor merely smirked, mocking her in front of the entire cast. It was her last act of defiance before her demise.

Detective Winston looked over his notepad. There was tension, anger and the revelation of betrayal. It wasn't lost on him that Elizabeth had not only lost her star actress but was facing a personal betrayal of unforgettable proportions. He had the facts, now his job was to uncover the truth. No matter how dark or sad it may be.

Detective Winston stroked his chin, hunched over the photos sprawled across his desk. The halberd lodged into Eleanor's chest had sent a chill through his spine. It wasn't every day that a wrestling ring turned murder scene with a halberd as the choice of weapon. The uniquely crafted design on the blade matched another one that he had seen before.

Lighting a cigarette, he recalls his conversation with the ex-husband. "I've never seen Freya without her sunglasses, man, not since we got hitched. She was always oddly sensitive to light."

"But let me tell you," the ex-husband continued, "when she did want to talk, she'd always insist on meeting at the park, on that bench overlooking the water. That's her style."

Winston had been waiting to talk to Freya at her usual spot, a park bench overlooking the water, when she finally approached. She sat down gingerly, sunglasses firmly over her eyes. True to her habit, she started the conversation.

"How can I help, Detective?" Freya kicked off the conversation, interrupting the peace offered by the chirping of birds nearby. 

"No pleasantries, huh?" Winston retorted, smoke billowing from the corner of his lips.

"What can I say, Winston? Let's get the ball rolling," Freya responded, avoiding his eyes. She seemed to shift uncomfortably, her gaze fixed on the passing ducks. Winston found it odd that she wouldn't make eye contact - a classic nervous trait - reminding him painfully of the ex-husband's remarks about her light sensitivity.

"You know about Eleanor's debt, right?"

Freya didn't bat an eyelid, just a sharp exhalation as she responded, "Yeah, I loaned her money for my historical artifact collection. She knew about my illegal artifact ventures... threatened to expose me if I didn't pay her back."

Winston blinked in surprise as he processed this information. Freya's bankruptcy declaration just last month floating to the front of his mind.

"Ahh, your historical artifacts... they wouldn't happen to include medieval weapons, would they? Like a halberd, with a similar design identical to the one used in Eleanor's murder?"

Freya's expression wrinkles as she nods, "Yeah, I take it every fortnight for maintenance... helps keep my combat training sharp too."

There it was, the fact he was waiting to unravel - the halberd used in the murder was indeed identical to the one in Freya's collection.

With that, he stands, dropping his cigarette butt into a nearby bin, leaving Freya on her usual park bench, hiding behind her sunglasses.

Background files from related investigations (some may be irrelevant):

In the heart of the rainforest, Jesse meets his gruesome end by a lawnmower, leaving Detective Winston embarked on a puzzling quest with suspects - Sam and Steve.

Detective Winston stood at the edge of the rainforest, reviewing his notes. The scene was grim, even for a seasoned detective. The body of Jesse, a young boy, had been found. The murder weapon, found near his body, was a lawnmower, an odd choice for a murder weapon, especially in a rainforest.

One suspect was Jesse's fellow schoolmate, Sam. His name had surfaced around the investigation thanks to a tip-off from the school janitor. The man remembered seeing Sam at the lost and found desk, writing something.

It appears that Sam had found some incriminating texts on his girlfriend's phone, all of which were sent by Jesse. When confronted, Sam's girlfriend confessed that she had been seeing Jesse behind Sam's back. This all coincided with the fact that Sam had access to paper and pen during his visit to the lost and found desk. Winston also learned that the numbers from the confiscated phones were noted down on a piece of paper.

The field trip group Sam and Jesse were part of were the only ones in the rainforest that day. Sam was among them, having also been given special privileges, being the only student allowed to access the lost and found box. Winston made yet another note of it. 

"Winston," a fellow detective called out, causing Winston to look up. 

"What is it?" He asked, heading towards the man.

"Just wanted you to know, we've seized the phones. The numbers were written down."

"On paper?"

The detective nodded, "Yeah. At the lost and found desk, from what we've heard."

Winston's eyes squinted as he thought. He knew these facts were significant, but their connection was not clear. 

"Okay. Thanks." Giving him a nod, he moved towards his vehicle. 

His mind whirled with facts as he started the car. Conversations with Sam, his fellow schoolmate's murder, confessions from his girlfriend, and peculiar facts from a field trip in the rainforest. 

He knew his job wasn't done until he found justice for Jesse, until he was able to connect the dots and bring the story together. For now, he just needed to keep gathering facts and truths. 

Every puzzle piece counted.

Rain pattered on the windshield as detective Winston drove toward the rainforest. A call had come in, a body, Jesse's, found in the woods. As the victims' details appeared on his screen in flickering neon blue, Winston registered one significant point that had yet to be confirmed - the murder weapon was a lawnmower.

Upon arriving at the scene, he climbed out of the car, his shoes squishing and sliding in the mud. It was time to pay a visit to the prime suspect, Steve, a dedicated Rabbi trying to make ends meet.

His visit to Steve was brief but loaded with significant information. To the unsuspecting, Steve was a devout religious leader and a generous individual who devoted his time to frequent forest clean-ups, never too busy to lend a hand with his own set of lawnmowers.

"Lately, my congregation has been dwindling, " Steve confessed. "I had to set up a lawn care business to support myself and the synagogue."

While Steve rambled, Winston learned more about Jesse's aggressive approach to business. "Jesse... he had an ambitious streak. I couldn't compete," Steve admitted, "He was systematically undercutting my prices, offering ridiculous summer discounts and premium services."

This confirmed Winston's suspicion that Jesse had not only been a rival but was planning to put Steve out of business. Steve, however, was not unaware. He suspected Jesse of stealing his clientele and provided evidence to Winston. Steve's business was shrinking while Jesse's was blooming, a fact evidenced by the bitterness lurking in the Steve's voice whenever Jesse was mentioned.

Winston, maintaining a stone face, asked about Steve's activities on the day of the murder. As if on cue, Steve informed him that there was a clean-up event on that same fateful day, occurring at the exact time Jesse met his grisly end.

Officers at the scene had confirmed the unusual chains of Steve's lawnmower as the cause of death. Oddly enough, Steve owned several lawnmowers, all part of his lawn care business, and he was more than proficient in their operation.

As Winston drove away, he filed away the various pieces of this entangled puzzle. With Steve's confession, Jesse's ambitious undercutting plan, Steve's rapidly decreasing list of clientele, and the coinciding timing of the clean-up event, this case was far from over.

When the silver screen flickered with an unexpected explosion, claiming the life of innocent Chloe, seasoned Detective Winston stepped in to unravel the deadly scandal entwining suspects Ruby and Roscoe.

Stepping through the bustling crime scene of a movie theater, Winston drew deeply on his cigarette, turning over the few facts he had. It was a terrible scene involving a grenade explosion, a midnight movie, and a tragedy. Winston ran a hand over his tired face as he recollected the events of the night. The victim, Chloe, had invited Ruby, a local psychic with a unique talent of foreseeing dangerous situations in her visions, to the movies. In the past, these visions had often involved violent scenes where weapons like grenades were used, a dangerous gift she suspected was influenced by her military background.

They'd stayed until the late night showing ended, and witnesses mentioned they were the last to leave. They also confirmed that none other individuals were seen entering or exiting the theater. 

Winston made his way to the torn-up cinema, stooping to look at the grenaded remains. The air was still heavy with the acrid residue of the explosion. Ruby, the psychic. Ruby, the military veteran. He suppressed a shudder as he thought about the fatalities she might have presaged in her past, with the shadow of a grenade always lingering in her visions, all too accurate.

In situations like these, she could have known how to handle a grenade, her service in the military would have ensured that. He had heard about this psychic's history. Ruby's accuracy was unsettling... Her record of predicting family tragedies had created an odd mix of fear and respect amongst her kin. They were a superstitious lot, some even believed that her visions were causing the very catastrophes she prophesied.

Winston beckoned an officer over, borrowing his notepad and pen to jot down some reminders. Ruby was last seen with Chloe. Ruby went to her brother’s house after the movie - The brother, who also happens to be an arms dealer.

Winston made his way to Ruby's apartment for an interview. Ruby had a feral look about her - her argument with her mother had clearly shaken her. She had decided to break off contact with her family after that blowout. Both of them seemed to be quite stubborn.

"Ruby," Winston began, "Can you tell me about the last time you saw Chloe?" He asked, his steely gaze fixing on her. 

"Yes, Detective. We watched a movie together. It ran late, we both stayed until the end." Ruby replied.

"And after the movie?" Winston probed.

"I... I went to visit my brother. He sells... various products. I remember when we played with toy soldiers as children..." Ruby’s voice trailed off, an odd glint in her eyes. 

Keeping his inquisitive gaze steady, Winston made his leave, leaving Ruby and her prophecies, often echoing with the sound of pin-pulled grenades, alone with the evening shadows.

Winston rubbed his temples as he sifted through the mountain of paperwork on his desk. What a way to spend his Sunday, pouring over case files and suspect lists. He moved onto the next file on his desk: Roscoe, an astrophysicist by day, apparent drug addict by night. 

His astrophysics job had Roscoe planted in a military base, which was known to have an arsenal that included grenades, for research purposes. Here, he utilized his broad scientific background including physics and chemistry. Although he normally processed information in a meticulous and scientific manner, witness testimonies painted a different picture altogether. Apparently, Roscoe had been acting erratically lately. Having a quick look at his employee records, Winston saw a slew of complaints piled up within the last few weeks. 

Roscoe's troubles found their way outside of the workplace, into a small apartment where he was the tenant. When the police were called for a noise complaint, they found drug paraphernalia scattered across the living room. Surely, his military career would see its last days if word got out. 

Winston sighed, leaning back in his chair, skimming through his notes. He paused at the mention of a late-night movie. Chloe, the unfortunate victim, had been Roscoe's unsuspecting companion in the dark theater. Just as the opening credits rolled, her life had been cut short by a grenade. 

Witness statements gathered at the scene confirmed that Roscoe had purchased a ticket for the same movie screening just moments before it began. Someone had seen him enter the theater, seemingly in a hurry. 

"These cases just keep getting trickier," Winston muttered to himself, downing another cup of coffee. His eyes moved to another statement, this time by one of Chloe's friends. It seemed that Chloe was about to report Roscoe's drug addiction to his superiors.

Winston called Roscoe's workplace. "Is that Roscoe's current position?" he asked the person on the other end. "Have you noticed anything... odd about his behavior lately?" He listened carefully to the responses, his face impassive.

"No further questions," Winston said as he bid goodbye and hung up the office phone. He then picked up another folder from the desk, ready to tackle the next round of information.

Target case file:

When Joel's life was abruptly ended by a nunchaku at the local bowling alley, it is up to Detective Winston to interrogate the prime suspects: Rosemary and Mia, in this chilling game of strike or spare.

Kneading the stub of his cigarette into the worn-out ashtray, Winston's gaze flitted between the photographs in front of him. A bowling alley, deserted, save for a solitary figure slumped over in the congealing slick of his own blood – the scene drenched in a chilling morbidity. 

His suspect was Mia, a waitress at the bowling alley. The late shift was her domain; her eyes, always heavy-lidded with fatigue, had fallen on a familiar figure, Joel, numbingly often. The man had his peculiar habits, including late-night bowling. Mia had a keen knowledge of that; it wasn’t easy to overlook when they regularly crossed paths during her shifts, Joel’s ball thundering and skidding down the shiny lanes.

Fiddling with a small, old key on his desk, Winston’s thought went back to his first meeting with Mia. He had found the key while cleaning her table after an interview and asked her about it. Almost flippantly, she mentioned it was for a private mausoleum in the nearby cemetery. The location was within walking distance from her workplace, an old cemetery cloaked in a gloom that seemed centuries old. The eerie part was her odd ritual; post her shift, her coworkers attested to seeing her trudge towards the graveyard regularly, a private pilgrimage in the dead of night.

Winston vividly remembered his surprise when he had found nunchaku, a pair of them, while searching Mia's home. The night visits to the cemetery coupled with the ominous presence of the martial arts weapon was undoubtedly unsettling. Unraveling further, he found out Mia had been practicing and honing her skills with the nunchaku at home, late into the night. For years, she had been devoted to martial arts, with a particular emphasis on the nunchaku, the significance of which crept up on him like a poisonous vine. Her gym was known for teaching the use of this weapon.

"I suspect you're quite adept at swinging these," Winston had said to Mia, gesturing towards the nunchaku that lay on the table between them when he'd confronted her about it later. 

Mia had smiled enigmatically, her eyes twinkling with the lethality of secrets untold. "Keep your eyes open, detective," she had replied, her voice a chilling sotto voce lingering between them, hang enough in the suffocating silence.

His thoughts whirling, Winston stubbed out the last of his cigarette. The available evidence was yet to form a coherent story, but Mia was conspicuous. He had ventured into labyrinthian investigations before, but the mystery of Joel's murder felt like uncharted territory. Winston felt a shiver creep into his spine as he got ready for round two with Mia.

Winston stepped into the dimly lit bowling alley, prowling between lanes like a panther on the hunt. An unusual place to be hammered to death, he thought, especially during the graveyard shift, but a good detective never questioned the chosen venues or the hour of the city's grim reaper. Winston surveyed the empty building, the only sound being that of his own boots echoing off the polished hardwood.

The bartender, one Rosemary – if her nameplate could be trusted – was scrubbing down a countertop at the far corner of the bar. Winston walked over, took a seat on one of the bar stools and introduced himself. 

"I hear you were working here the night Joel was killed," he mentioned, as he watched her movements. 

Rosemary looked up, her face impassive, "Yes, that's true. It was my usual midnight shift, and Joel got murdered after we had closed down for the night. Wasn't much else to do."

"You seem to have keys to this place," Winston noticed, spotting a set of keys on the counter. 

"Yes, I do, for closing hours," she replied, sliding the keys back into her jeans pocket.

He continued his questions, "I understand you practice martial arts, Rosemary?"

For the first time, Rosemary stopped her cleaning and smiled, "Yes, that's right. In fact, I work out regularly at a martial arts gym. Nunchaku workshops are my favorite," she added, her eyes twinkling with something akin to pride.

Winston nodded, imparting no judgement on her preferred pastime. 

Suddenly, a glint at the corner of the room caught his attention. A collection of weaponry displayed on a wall. Upon closer look, he recognized various martial arts weapons, including a pair of nunchaku.

“My father was a big fan of martial arts. He left me his collection," explained Rosemary, noticing his interest. "In fact, the nunchaku you see hanging on the wall is part of my personal collection."

As Winston stood up to leave, he turned to Rosemary, "Did you know Joel well?"

She hesitated for a moment, her eyes downcast, "Joel... he was a good friend. He always wanted to help. And he was the one person who could save me from this terrible debt I'm wrestling with. But to my despair, he... he said no when I asked him for a loan."

As Winston exited the empty bowling alley, he couldn't help but mull over Rosemary's last words. This was shaping up to be a long investigation, a fact he was all too aware of as he walked into the piercing chill of the night cityscape.
question: Who is the most likely murderer?

context:
Background files from related investigations (some may be irrelevant):

In an adrenaline inducing bungee jumping site, Mack's thrill-seeking adventure came to a gruesome end by a nunchaku; now, it's up to Detective Winston to unravel the deadly secrets between Mackenzie and Ana.

Winston sat quietly in an unmarked Ford, parked a block away from Mackenzie's downtown apartment building. He observed Mackenzie through his binoculars, watching closely as they hastily unlocked their front door. It had been a long day at the office for Mackenzie and, like clockwork, they were seen taking their customary break on a public bench, working on their laptop.

Before long, Mackenzie was seen through the partially closed blinds of their apartment, sitting at their desk with their laptop open. They had just returned from a local cyber security meetup, a reality Winston discovered after following Mackenzie to the event later that evening. As Winston watched, they shifted their body and their eyes darted around, Winston duly noted on Mackenzie's apparent concern for online privacy.

"Interesting," Winston thought, while making a mental note to do some research on further cyber security meetups occurring in the vicinity.

The next morning, Winston watched Mackenzie walk out of a martial arts training center. As Mackenzie stopped to say goodbye to their instructor, Winston quickly snapped a photo on his phone. In the picture, Winston could clearly see Mackenzie practicing techniques with the unmistakable form of Mackenzie's sturdy nunchaku resting in the backdrop. This gave Winston a clue that his martial arts training includes nunchaku techniques.

Winston's interest peaked further when he followed Mackenzie to a local shop where they were seen purchasing a new set of nunchaku. Even more intriguing was when they examined a pair of cufflinks on display with a yearning look, cufflinks Winston knew were identical to a pair Mack frequently flaunted around. It appeared Mack had things that Mackenzie also desired.

The investigator decided it was time to pay Mackenzie a visit. He knocked on the apartment door and Mackenzie cautiously invited him in.

Pleasantries were briefly exchanged before Winston's gaze quickly fell on the laptop that was resting by some papers next to an open window.

"You always take this with you to work?" Winston inquired, pointing at the laptop.

"Every day," Mackenzie replied, "I can't leave my work at the office."

"Work goes that well, huh?" Winston probed further. "I hear you were recently ... overlooked for a promotion."

At these words, Mackenzie's expression darkened. "I was the top candidate, you know. It should've been mine. Mack, the new guy, he is nothing compared to me, but he takes it. That promotion, the respect I had. Even those cufflinks I have always wanted, somehow Mack always gets to have them."

Winston nodded, making a mental note of Mackenzie's reaction. They turned the conversation to martial arts and during the chat, Mackenzie unintentionally revealed their prowess with nunchaku.

In a small, hidden compartment in Mackenzie's wardrobe, Winston found the pair of nunchaku that Mackenzie had recently purchased. He swiftly snapped a picture of this evidence before closing the wardrobe.

As the day grew late, Winston thanked Mackenzie for their time and headed out, feeling more certain than ever about the path his investigation was following.

Winston sat in his office, photos of Mack --the bungee jumper found dead-- scattered heartbreakingly across his desk. The lack of clues at the murder site puzzled him, nothing seemed out of place. All he had was an unusual weapon, the nunchaku, not something he’d found at too many crime scenes.

Standing up, he straightened his tie and headed to the shared housing complex of the victim and suspect. Ana Diaz lived here, along with Mack. Ground rules for questioning the suspect were laid out in his mind.

Ana received him with a stoic expression and invited him inside. Her suitcase was unpacked, strewn helter-skelter around the room. She explained she had come back from the bungee jumping site late last night, still in shock about Mack’s murder.

Nunchaku lay on the table. Winston noticed, she explained it as the normal household item of a martial artist. She said she practices martial arts at the same bungee jumping location. 

Asked about their shared occupation, she sighed heavily. “Mack loved it, though," She said, "He was the instigator, insisting everyone take the jump.”

Ana seemed to soften, talking about her faith, her traditions. “Bungee jumping, it's against my beliefs,” she admitted, “but I’d signed up too, expecting some ridicule like always.”

Ridicule. That was a word Winston had already heard before concerning Mack. He asked around, among their friends, everyone said the same, Mack liked to joke, to point fun at beliefs. Especially Ana’s it seemed.

They left together, Ana and Mack, the morning of the murder, people had seen them. Winston asked why, given their strained relationship. Ana shrugged off, her hands trembling. “He wasn’t too bad,” she replied. 

Nobody else was documented at the bungee jumping site that day, only Mack and Ana. It was time to head there. Winston thanked Ana for her time and left, driving straight to the scene. He stared up at the looming diving board, picturing the scene.  

Only two people there that day, Mack and Ana. He looked around, the martial arts practice ground nearby held the last piece. Nunchaku, a common weapon in martial arts practices. He tested one, the weight fitting neatly into his palm while he surveyed the area. This was the scene he needed to piece together.

In the tranquil sphere of the temple, Charlotte's demise by barbed wire disrupts the serenity, drawing Detective Winston into a puzzling web woven by suspects Priscilla and Xenia.


Winston unfolded the clipped newspaper announcement of Charlotte's upcoming wedding. He scanned the quaint details, turning each over in his mind. The setting was a temple, a peculiar choice within their community. Unique also, was the choice of Xenia as the wedding planner. A woman known for her fastidiousness and deft hands in crafting seamless events. 

In a recent chat with Charlotte before her wedding, she mentioned a peculiar detail regarding a certain secret she was advised by Xenia to keep hidden - her past relationship with Xenia's current partner. It was a secret she was planning to unveil at the altar, a revelation that would surely raise a few eyebrows, with Xenia no longer being the lone keeper of it.

"Ms. Xenia, I presume?" Winston asked, entering the wedding planner's office. 

"Yes. How can I aid you detective?" Xenia responded, with a slight surprise in her eyes.

"I wanted to talk about Charlotte's wedding... a ceremony that was slated to occur at the exact minute of her murder. Noticed anything unusual around those days?” Winston queried.

Xenia hesitated, her expression wavering. It was clear that the jab about Charlotte's intention to confess the past, which involved Xenia's significant other, had struck a nerve. The anger simmering in Xenia's eyes was volatile and intense, enough to make anyone uncomfortable.

As they conversed, Winston's attention drifted to an office closet, slightly ajar. A suitcase peeked from within, stuffed with neatly folded clothes, almost as though it was constantly ready for a trip. His colleagues had often mentioned seeing this suitcase during their routine meetings with Xenia.

"Ever much of a traveler, Xenia?" Winston asked casually. 

She seemed taken aback by his question. "Sometimes... it's part of the job. Last minute trips for a desired decoration, or perhaps to get a gift. Weekend trips and all."

"That your suitcase in the closet, always packed and ready?" Winston nodded towards it. Xenia followed his gaze toward the suitcase, then back at him. "Yes, why?" 

"No reason," Winston shrugged. "It’s just that colleagues have mentioned spotting you with your luggage at the airport, and at the train station buying tickets – during work hours."

"Yeah, like I said, travelling becomes part of the job sometimes,” countered Xenia, smoothly.

Throughout their conversation about wedding preparations, Xenia specified that she was responsible for every minute detail – setting up and breaking down the décor, liaising with the temple people, overseeing every aspect of the event. She emphasized that her duties required her presence before, during, and after the ceremony. Winston mentally jotted this down, noticing how neatly these timings coincided with those of Charlotte's unfortunate fate.

Winston rose to depart, conveying his gratitude, "Thanks for your time."

"Of course, anything to help," Xenia replied softly. “Charlotte's passing is shocking, but remember, we rely on trust and reputation in our business. It's all we have. Charlotte's confession could have marred that."

Detective Winston sifted through the papers littering his desk. Crime scene photos mixed with witness statements and information on both the victim, Charlotte, and the potential suspect, Priscilla. Winston ran a hand through his hair, taking a deep breath.

Eyewitness accounts placed Priscilla at the temple on the day of the crime. The same temple where Charlotte was found, her life taken by barbed wire. Winston's gaze drifted towards some photos of the hiking trails Priscilla was known to frequent. The trails, all too often, wound their way past the same temple where Charlotte met her end.

Pushing the papers around, Winston found a report from the local police. Priscilla's involvement with certain gang activities was far from a well-kept secret. The faded gang tattoos on Priscilla's skin were testament to her affiliation. Charlotte, on the other hand, was part of a rival gang, a fact anyone could see from the tags she left behind. 

Photos from the trails Priscilla often hiked showed a significant amount of barbed wire fencing. Winston mused, barbed wire was indeed common along these trails - so much so that Priscilla had even learned to utilize items like it in her own survival knowledge on these hiking expeditions. 

A picture of Priscilla hiking caught Winston's attention. He noted the pair of wire snips she carried. Those would be potentially useful in dealing with the surplus of barbed wire on her usual trails. He also noted the rough timeline on the police report. Charlotte's time of death matched up too neatly with the time witnesses had spotted Priscilla at the temple that day.

"Interesting, isn't it?" Winston muttered to himself, mulling over the facts at hand. Pushing his chair back, he decided it was time to ask Priscilla some questions. He was determined to learn the truth, one piece of evidence at a time.

In the glimmering lights and pulsating bass of the local roller rink, Wendy met her brutal end with a pickaxe, leaving Detective Winston the unenviable task of untangling suspect stories from Marianne and Sidney.

Detective Winston tapped his pen against the mugshot of Marianne. She wore the hardened expression of a seasoned miner, and a sprinkle of white dust beaded her forehead. She had, years ago, spent a considerable amount of time underground before she traded the pickaxe for a ring. Even after her marriage, however, Winston knew that Marianne was not unfamiliar with the heft and purpose of such a tool.

His eyes consisted of the audit papers laid out before him, declaring a significant debt that Marianne owed in back taxes. She was circling financial demise, and the state was closing in. Then, his eyes shifted to the statement provided by a friend of hers, highlighting her strong assertion that she would rather perish than get sent behind bars. It seemed to Winston that Marianne was still filled with the spirits of the old miners, willing to risk it all in pursuit of her own freedom.

His venture out to her parcel of land a few days back had stamped the image in his mind of her mining tools lounging out in the open. They were well-kept and clean, the way old miners kept their tools. Marianne had been spotted around the community with the pickaxe, using it for various garden works and general maintenance.

Now Winston's attention moved to Wendy, the victim, an honest lady known for her earnest ways. She was found in a sequestered section of the roller rink, a roller skate still hanging onto her foot as if she was frozen mid-skate.

Placing a call, Winston requested the CCTV footage of the roller rink from the night of the murder. There, in the flickering low resolution, was Wendy locked in a heated argument with Marianne. The dispute ended and Wendy skated off, but Marianne stayed.

Later, another clip showed Marianne lingering along the outskirts, long after the other skaters had left. It was an eerie sight - the roller rink was empty, except for the flickering neon lights and Marianne, circling the rink with an unsettling calmness.

Winston slid an envelope towards himself and carefully extracted a photograph. It was Wendy's last piece of brave detective work - a picture of Marianne caught in a grim action that served as undeniable proof of her crime. But it was Wendy, with her unwavering integrity, who held this tight to her chest, vowing to expose the truth about Marianne.

Two cups of coffee empty, Winston switched off the lights and left the room. The image of Marianne and the pickaxe lingered in the darkness of the office, the unsaid words and whispers of the CCTV footage bouncing off the walls. The unwelcome truth seemed to have found a perfect partner with the impending dawn, unflinching and relentless.

As Winston flipped through the case file, his eyes landed on a photo of the crime scene. His heart ached slightly for the young woman, Wendy, brutally murdered at the roller rink. The weapon of choice: a pickaxe. Not something you would typically see at a roller rink.

Entering the rink, Winston felt a shudder creep up his spine as he glanced at the spot where Wendy's body had been found. Shaking off his unease, he made his way over to the row of lockers where the staff pointed him to Sidney's locker.

It was well known that Sidney, a local geologist, was a regular at this establishment. Even given the oddity of a geologist frequenting a roller rink, Winston was familiar enough with murder investigations to understand that people, like rocks, had layers. 

Casually, Winston made conversation, "You're here a lot, I hear?" Sidney nodded, almost dismissively, not yet prepared to show his hand. "I heard you often chat about your friend Jack, is that right?" Sidney nodded again, this time more cautiously.

"I find skating to be a wonderful escapism," Sidney murmured, while scanning the rink with a haunted look. His guard dropped slightly as he added, "And Jack...well, you know about Jack and his troubles."

From an interrogation room in the local precinct, Jack, a known criminal and Sidney's friend, gazed at Winston. Already serving time, he had nothing to lose by divulging information. As Sidney’s name left Winston's lips, Jack's eyes grew wide.

"He's a letter writer, you know. Always has been," Jack offered, unprompted. Winston thought curiously about the possible relevance of this. Jack continued, now with a dropped voice, "He cherishes the art of placing words on paper."

Caught off guard by the reverence in Jack's words, Winston's attention piqued at the news that Sidney was a common pen pal.

At the roller rink office, Sidney's tormented expression flitted across the screen of the surveillance camera footage. There he was with Wendy, both laughing and skating. The timestamp below the image – the night of Wendy’s death. As the staff had mentioned, Sidney’s presence during the hours coinciding with the murder fit. There was little doubt that he had been in the vicinity.

Winston packed his notepad away and left for Sidney's apartment. There, the detective found an abundance of stamps and stationary stacked neatly by the desk. A typewriter nearby indicated an air of old-school character. Jack's words suddenly resurfaced. Scanning the room again, Winston spotted a picture of Wendy. Beside it, a letter with Sidney's handwriting.

Hands in his slick black overcoat pockets, Winston glanced around the roller rink one last time before leaving. Stopping at the doorway, he turned around to Sidney, opening his mouth to say something before deciding against it. Winston remembered their previous conversation. "I have no idea what Wendy was talking about," Sidney had said defiantly when confronted with the secret Wendy had been spreading about him.

Suddenly, Winston remembered what he had heard in side conversations with Wendy's friends. The secret she knew wasn't just ruinous; it was humiliating. She knew something that, once revealed, would publicly disgrace Sidney. 
                    
With a sigh, he discarded the thought and walked out into the chill of the evening. His mind buzzed with unanswered questions. There was more to this case. More to Sidney. More to Wendy. To think it all revolved around a roller rink. He'll crack it open, he always does.

Background files from related investigations (some may be irrelevant):

When renowned dancer Nathaniel is found dead, struck by a blowgun dart in his own studio, it's up to Detective Winston to interrogate the only two suspects: Homer the janitor and Clara, Nathaniel’s star pupil.

Winston extinguished his half-smoked cigar and sorted through the papers littering his desk. Most of them bore information about Nathaniel's untimely demise in a local dance studio.

Nathaniel, an outgoing character with a dubious financial psyche, earned people's ire quite often. He apparently had it big for stealing shiny things. Of note was Clara’s valuable pearl necklace, which he was rumoured to be in possession of.

Winston thought it was apt time to pay Clara a visit.

Nathaniel and Clara; cousins by parental lineage, contrasting dramatically by nature. While Clara was reserved, she carried a fervour for dancing. A known face at the dance studios. Heck, she was last seen near the studio just before the mishap unfolded. Winston pondered whether this was chance or circumstance.

Reaching her apartment, Winston knocked and Clara greeted him. He noticed a throwing dart board in the hallway with clusters of darts piercing the centre.

“Fancy playing darts?” he asked casually.

“My favourite pastime,” Clara replied, the faintest light dancing in her eyes. Winston gestured towards the bullseyes, “You're quite good then.” Clara just smiled in response.

Winston recalled her reputation of playing dart games in the locale, consistently hitting bulls-eye.

Winston changed the subject, "Your cousin was rumoured to have your pearl necklace. Is that correct?" Clara gave him a curt nod and recounted the time she caught Nathaniel sporting her missing necklace. "I was outraged!"

A glint of vulnerability in Clara’s eyes didn’t escape Winston’s scrutiny.

The conversation veered towards charities, with a quick detour to a mention about her cousin, the hunter. She confided in Winston about a fraudulent charity she’d invested heavily in. She later found out Nathaniel operated the charity.

Winston took this opportunity to broach the subject of her sighting at her cousin the hunter’s house on the murder day.

“Indeed, I had to pick up a few things,” Clara replied candor in her voice.

On his way out, Winston stopped by the darts board. His gaze rested on the bullseyes and then fleetingly on an antique blowgun displayed above the nearby mantelpiece.

“From the hunter’s collection?” he asked, veiling the touch of interest in his tone.

“All part of the family,” Clara replied.

As he drove back, the facts played in his mind. Clara and her lost pearl necklace, her surprising accuracy with darts, her visit to the hunter’s house and her being in close vicinity of the dance studio where Nathaniel was found dead. He had a lot to think about.

Detective Winston paced around his office, going over the information he had collected thus far on Nathaniel's peculiar death in the dance studio. His mind kept circling back to Homer, the victim's financial advisor, who owned an impressive collection of various hunting equipment that intriguingly enough, included multiple blowguns.

Nathaniel had found some suspicious discrepancies in his accounts and was bold enough to confront Homer about it. It didn't sit right with Winston. But again, his job was to look at facts, not reach conclusions.

Homer was a perplexing personality. Winston remembered him asking about his dietary preferences during their first encounter. With a nonchalant shrug, Homer didn't have much to say about meat or vegetables. Not that it mattered half as much as the other facts on Winston's desk.

His trips to observe Homer didn't paint any brighter a picture. He'd seen Homer practice his blowgun skills. His neighbors had reported hearing nocturnal hunting noises from Homer's home. This didn't surprise Winston given Homer's past in the special forces, where he'd been trained to use such exotic weapons.

But practice was one thing, shopping quite another. Winston had had some surveillance on Homer and saw him, on one occasion, purchasing what looked astonishingly like a blowgun in a local hunting store.

There were also those mysterious letters. They'd been signed off anonymously but were traced back to Nathaniel. The letters were cloyingly demanding, asking for large sums of money. Homer refused to elaborate on them, much as he hadn't provided any reasoning for the financial discrepancies Nathaniel had discovered.

Winston let out a sigh, pushing his glasses up on his nose. He'd been through all the information, and he couldn't shake off the nagging feeling that he needed to look deeper. But again, that wasn't his call to make. He'd leave it up to others to decide if Homer was just an eccentric hunter or whether the venom was from his blowgun. His job here was done.

When Howard was found dead in his home office, strangled by a coil of barbed wire, it fell to Detective Winston to sift through lies of the prime suspects: Eric and Priscilla.

Winston sighed as he glanced at the report of the latest murder. Howard, killed in his home office, and with barbed wire of all things. Admittedly, he wasn't an animal lover, but the fact the murderer was brazen enough to use something like that was unnerving.

Getting out of his car, he approached the home of his latest suspect, Eric. A pet groomer by trade, who Howard had hired frequently to look after his pets. The peculiar thing about Eric was not only that he used barbed wire to fence the more adventurous pets in check, but that he always carried his work tools, barbed wire included, to his clients' homes. 

A neighbor had once mentioned how often he'd seen Eric hauling his grooming tools to his van, barbed wire coils included, and he frequently overheard the sound of water running from Eric's place, leading to reports of an unusually high water bill for Eric last month. The bill was discussed by the locals, and how this pet groomer used a lot of water in his duties wasn't lost on them.

Winston knocked on the door, greeted by a man with sincere eyes and the faint smell of animal shampoo.

“You're Eric, right?” said Winston.

“That’s correct” the man replied with a friendly smile.

"And you groom pets, correct?" Winston continued.

"That's right. I love animals. Even work with barbed wire to keep the more... adventurous ones in check. People in the neighborhood could tell you that. My next-door neighbor always sees me taking my work tools, including the wire, to my clients' homes and he hears the water running as well. You know, cause of bathing and grooming."

“Hmm,..." Winston hummed, rubbing his chin thoughtfully. "You ever work at Howard's place?"

“Of course!" Eric exclaimed quickly. "Known him, his fiancee Gloria, and his pets for a while now. Have them on top of my customer list, along with a large number of other cat and dog owners.”

“Gloria?” Winston probed.

Eric's face flushed, “Yes, I've known her for years, almost ten now. I visit her often for work, and...”

"Anything else about Gloria?" Winston interrupted.

Eric paused for a moment before responding, “She’s special, Gloria. Kind to everything and everyone, she often showed me signs of warmth and kindness."

As Winston observed Eric, he noticed a notebook lying open on a nearby table. Flipping to the appointments section, he found a number of entries for cat and dog owners, confirming Eric's busy schedule. One page, however, caught his attention: a diary page with 'I love Gloria' written numerous times, speaking volumes about Eric's feelings for her.

"Thank you for your time, Eric," Winston finally said. As he headed towards the door, he turned and asked, "Howard's office, fur on the barbed wire used?"

Eric nodded. "Yes, found it quite odd. Normally, I only groom pets in their homes."

Exiting the home, he made his way back to his car, a new collection of information swirling in his head. Winston had an uneasy feeling about this Eric. He made a mental note to have Eric’s diary and customer list with a number of cat and dog owners entered into evidence. There were a lot of dots to connect and they seemed to be dancing around in his head.

The blaring sirens came to a halt as Winston arrived at where the latest gruesome killing had taken place. Howard, a man who liked his quiet and often threw himself into work, found dead in his home office. According to initial reports, the murder weapon seemed to be a strand of barbed wire. Winston proceeded towards the crime scene, trying to keep his senses sharp to any clues he might find.

Priscilla was a person of interest in the case. Tied to a string of crimes that included the use of barbed wire, she seemed more suspicious with every detail. Winston would be remiss if he didn't get all the facts about her lined up and ready. Priscilla, an ex-military personnel, stood out for her lack of an alibi during the time of murder. Winston made a note to conduct a thorough interrogation.

While going over the diagrams and photos of the scene, Winston found that Howard's property was surrounded by barbed wire fences. An odd detail to his suburban house. Witnesses - the neighbors- reported seeing Priscilla's car on multiple occasions, and explicitly during the time of the murder, at the fenced property. A regular visitor, it seemed. Priscilla had no alibi, and knew the layout of the house well.

Howard, always a reserved man, chose to spend lengthy hours alone in his home office. The numerous sightings of Priscilla at his house during these late work hours, and decisively at the time of murder, intrigued Winston. These were little crumbs, but they pointed Winston in a strong direction.

Winston pulled Priscilla in for questioning; she was not an easy nut to crack. She had a history, pervasions into criminal activities that increased her confidence in her ability to avoid capture. Murmurings of previous killings involving barbed wire whirled around her, and each successful kill reportedly fed her sense of power and precision.

Winston’s revelations grew more unnerving when he discovered that Howard, knowing too much, had threatened to turn her in to the authorities. A direct threat, a motive. Could she have killed Howard to protect her dark secrets? Unraveling Priscilla's role in this was going to be a daunting task that Winston had to muster the strength to undertake. Hidden somewhere amidst these scattered pieces of evidence was the truth, waiting to be pieced together.

Target case file:

In the glitz and glamour of a bustling casino, a deadly secret unfolds as Iris is found lifeless by a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston with two puzzling suspects - Madison and Christine.

Winston struck a match, lighting his pipe and eyeing his case files splayed out on the desk before him. He had a slight headache after a long day of looking into the mysterious death of a lady called Iris. A sad story really, she was a frequent visitor at the casino, she had the luck of a devil. She often walked out of that place with a smile on her face and a hefty amount in her purse...until the night she didn't walk out at all.

Sifting through the evidence, Winston's hand found an envelope labeled 'Confidential.' Inside, there was a recorded statement Iris had given to a trusted friend a few days before her death. Iris clearly expressed her intention to report Christine at her next police visit.

The only real link he had to the case so far was Christine. Christine was a solid, muscular woman who worked long hours at a construction site. It wasn't just her construction job that kept her fit, it was also the time she spent with Iris working on a shared construction project. It was during these long hours they spent together that they built a strong association, a teamwork which often led them to the casino.

Christine, during one of their teamwork endeavors revealed to Iris her involvement in certain illicit activities. Iris, shocked by this revelation, clearly intended to report these activities to the police, a fact she expressed in the recorded statement Winston now held in his hands.

Another peculiar detail, a lead pipe -- the same type as the murder weapon -- was discovered at Christine and Iris's collective work site. Christine certainly had the brawn to wield that pipe.

Winston flipped open the file and spread out the still shots from the casino's surveillance footage. A timestamp in the corner corroborated with his notes -- Christine was present at the casino the night of the murder.

The police station was quiet as he entered Christine's holding cell. The woman looked tense but tried to put up a brave front.

"Spending a lot of time at the casino and the construction site these days?" He asked.

"Sure, ever since Iris and I started working on that project together. We often celebrated our small victories at the casino" Christine's voice choked a bit on her friend's name.

"And during those hours you told Iris about your...extra-curricular activities?" Winston pressed further. Christine didn't deny it, remained silent.

"Iris had planned to turn you in you know?" Winston said coolly, fanning out the recorded statement. "This was her intention during her upcoming visit to the police station."

Christine didn't respond, just locked her gaze onto Winston's.

"I noticed a lead pipe lying around your shared construction site, identical to the murder weapon," he pushed further. "Now, Christine, what else did you two discuss when you were working on those projects?"

Winston sat back, letting his words linger in the chill air of the interview room. The pieces of the puzzle were slowly falling into place, but the game was far from over.

Detective Winston scoured through the casino surveillance footage once again, his grim reflection faintly visible on the monitor screen. There was Madison, peering into what looked like a 'souvenir' box, a curious mix of nostalgia and uncertainty etched on their face. Not a lead, but perhaps another piece of the puzzle.

A separate clip caught Winston's eye, revealing Iris within the casino, merrily wagering lady luck amidst a sea of other gamblers. Iris and Madison under the same roof. It made sense something had transpired, but it was not his place yet to jump to conclusions.

Subsequent investigation took Winston to Madison's apartment. Reports had come in that they were often seen witnessing Iris's Friday night departures for the casino. Madison, it seemed, had an insight into Iris's late-night gambling endeavors, if only because they both shared the same neighborhood.

A new twist arrived in the form of an overheard conversation. Madison, just within earshot of Winston's position, seemed to be reminiscing about overhearing Iris's tales of the casino's allure. It didn't boost the investigation, but it added an interesting dynamic.

As the day wore on, Winston moved to the next building with a lead. Madison, seen using a key to enter the previous tenant's apartment, raised some questions. On being questioned about possessing this particular key, Madison nostalgically said, "Ah, such memories." The janitor confirmed that Madison had indeed requested a copy of the previous occupant's keys. A favor for an old friend or something more sinister?

The detective moved his inquiry to the legal hullabaloo that suddenly had Iris at the heart of it. Surveillance footage showed her in the courthouse with an armful of court documents. Iris was no ordinary casino patron but a key witness in a court case directly linked to Madison's illegal activities. This implied a new layer of complication to their association.

Legal terms printed on an eviction notice in Madison's possession stated that any illegal activities could lead to immediate eviction. Madison, having received this, was acutely aware of the implications of Iris' testimony.  A visit to the casino and the courthouse, another twist in the tale, was when Madison's lawyer had to break the news to their client about Iris's damning testimony.

But for Winston, there was still a bunch of questions left unanswered, and the jigsaw was only half complete. The investigation had to dig deeper. There was a long day ahead. Pieces were moving, and Winston knew well enough in this game; nothing moved without a reason.
